lead.headline: Queens files 27,940 income tax returns; the last received at 11:59:58 p.m.
lead.deck: 6,340 handed in at the Jamaica counter yesterday; four returns presented after midnight 'heard to be late'; Deputy Commissioner Corless to report to Albany
lead.body: The State Tax Commission's Queens office at Jamaica received 6,340 income tax returns for 1928 at its counter yesterday, bringing the borough's total to 27,940, Deputy Commissioner Hugh Corless states. The last return accepted was received at 11:59:58 p.m., the office's house system fixing the time. Four returns presented between midnight and 12:03 a.m. were recorded as late and will draw a penalty of 5 per cent. A queue of about 300 persons stood in Parsons Boulevard at 10 p.m.

columns.headline: Yankees open at the Stadium today against Boston; Exchange to carry the game
columns.body: The Yankees open the American League season at the Stadium at 3:30 p.m. today against the Boston club, the players wearing their numbers. The Queens Exchange will carry the play to subscribers on request. The Stadium's house system will measure the crowd 'against last year's opening.'

columns.headline: WORS 1610 not heard for a fifth night; launches to remain 'for the week'
columns.body: WORS 1610 has not been heard since 11:16 p.m. on April 10, when the transmission ended in mid-figure, Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states. The Division's three launches off North Beach, Hallett's Point and College Point will remain on station 'for the week.'

columns.headline: Ten couples remain at the marathon's 222nd hour; a Maspeth couple retires
columns.body: Ten couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 222nd hour, a couple from Maspeth having retired at 7:15 p.m. yesterday 'by mutual consent.' Dr. Saul Weisz reports Mrs. Margaret Corrigan 'sound in wind and poor in shoes.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Weather Bureau forecasts rain until afternoon; the Yankees' management will decide on the opening game at noon.

speaker.ear: Rain. High 52. Tuesday. No ball game. The Babe has other plans.

lead.headline: Rain calls the opener off, and the Yankees' numbers stay on hold
lead.deck: Huggins's numbered men sit in the clubhouse till twenty to two; the Stadium's register measures a drizzle; tomorrow, weather and the Babe permitting
lead.body: The season was to open at the Stadium at half past three this afternoon with the Yankees in their numbers, and at twenty to two the rain opened instead. Mr. Huggins called it off. Forty thousand people who had planned to be ill this afternoon must now be ill tomorrow. The Stadium's house system, set up to measure the crowd against last year's, measured a drizzle and a groundsman. The Babe left early in a closed car and would not say where he was going.

columns.headline: The tax man holds the line till midnight, and four callers ring off late
columns.body: Twenty-seven thousand nine hundred and forty Queens returns went in by midnight, the last with two seconds to spare. Four men arrived between midnight and three minutes past and were heard to be late, five per cent apiece. One blames his watch. The record blames the man.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Six nights of dead air, and Woodside misses the figures
columns.body: WORS has been off the air since Wednesday at sixteen past eleven, and Queens has noticed. The Exchange took ninety calls last night asking whether anybody else could hear nothing. The household on 61st Street has put a cloth over the set.

columns.headline: Mrs. Corrigan is down to her last soles, and dancing on them
columns.body: A Maspeth couple sat down by mutual consent at a quarter past seven, leaving ten. Dr. Weisz calls Mrs. Corrigan sound in wind and poor in shoes. Mr. Gant has offered her his. She has declined, his being worse. The band is on its fourth trombone.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The opener is set for tomorrow at half past three. The Weather Bureau has been asked to keep its hands to itself.

lead.headline: National Library of Wales cables Dr. Strand: the 23rd bar 'received and played'
lead.deck: Cable dated Aberystwyth 4:12 p.m. Tuesday; the Library asks for 'the twenty-two bars before it, sung'; Dr. Strand to record them at Union Seminary today
lead.body: The National Library of Wales has cabled Dr. Matthias Strand that the record of the 23rd bar of the WORS 1610 carol, sailed on the Berengaria on April 6, was 'received and played' at Aberystwyth on Monday. The cable, dated 4:12 p.m. Tuesday, reads in full: 'RECEIVED AND PLAYED. SEND TWENTY-TWO BARS BEFORE IT SUNG NOT TRANSMITTED. LETTER FOLLOWS.' Dr. Strand stated that he will record the first 22 bars at Union Seminary today.

columns.headline: President's message on farm relief read to the special session at noon
columns.body: President Hoover's message to the special session of Congress, proposing a Federal Farm Board with a revolving fund, was read to both houses at noon yesterday. The Queens Exchange carried the reading to 3,100 subscribers, of whom 212 'remained for the whole,' Superintendent Wilfred Arne states.

columns.headline: Opening game postponed at 1:40 p.m.; the Yankees to try again today
columns.body: The Yankees' opening game against the Boston club was postponed at 1:40 p.m. yesterday on account of rain, the club states. About 3,000 persons had entered the Stadium by that hour. The game will be played today at 3:30 p.m. if the field allows.

columns.headline: Nine couples remain at the 246th hour; the Arena's records fill a second office
columns.body: Nine couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 246th hour, the management states, a Woodhaven couple having retired at 11:20 p.m. The Arena's record of the contest now fills the box office and part of the manager's office, about 530 sides.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states; the Exchange logged 64 inquiries.

speaker.ear: Showers. High 56. Wednesday. Rain again. The Babe found something to do.

lead.headline: The Babe ties the knot at half past five, and keeps the church off the air
lead.deck: Mr. Ruth and Mrs. Hodgson wed at St. Gregory's before the milkmen are up; the church's system switched off by request; the opener rained out a second day
lead.body: At half past five this morning, while most of New York was still under its blankets, Mr. George Herman Ruth married Mrs. Claire Hodgson at St. Gregory the Great on West Ninetieth Street, and the church, at the couple's request, switched off its system and recorded nothing. About sixty early birds stood on the steps. They heard the organ through the door. Then it rained, and the opener was put off again. Mr. Huggins says tomorrow. Mrs. Ruth says she will be there.

columns.headline: Wales picks up the record, and rings back for the rest of the tune
columns.body: The National Library of Wales has played Dr. Strand's twenty-third bar and cabled for the twenty-two before it, sung, not transmitted. A letter follows. Dr. Strand spent the afternoon at Union Seminary singing them into a machine. He says the letter will say what it says.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is the farm message still holding?'
columns.body: Sir, the President's message on farm relief was read to Congress at noon and put through to three thousand one hundred Queens subscribers, of whom two hundred and twelve stayed to the end. The operator was one. She has views on revolving funds and will share them for a nickel.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Sixty-four callers ask after a station that won't pick up
columns.body: Sixty-four people rang the Exchange last night to ask whether WORS was on. It was not. The operator told each of them so, kindly. One lady in Hunters Point says she cannot sleep without the figures and has taken to counting her own. She got to four hundred.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Nine couples left at the Arena. The Arena has run out of room for the records and begun stacking them in the cloakroom.

lead.headline: Mr. Ruth married at 5:30 a.m. at St. Gregory's; opening game again postponed
lead.deck: Mrs. Claire Hodgson the bride; the church system 'not engaged, at the parties' request'; the Yankees and Boston to play today at 3:30 p.m.
lead.body: Mr. George Herman Ruth of the Yankees was married to Mrs. Claire Merritt Hodgson at 5:30 a.m. yesterday at the Church of St. Gregory the Great, West 90th Street, Manhattan, before about 60 persons on the steps. The church's house system was 'not engaged, at the parties' request,' the rectory states. The ceremony lasted about 15 minutes. The Yankees' opening game against Boston was postponed for rain at 1:15 p.m. for the second day and will be played today at 3:30 p.m.

columns.headline: Radio Division withdraws two of its three launches; North Beach to remain
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that the Division's launches off Hallett's Point and College Point will be withdrawn today, WORS 1610 not having been heard since 11:16 p.m. on April 10. The North Beach launch 'will remain until further notice.'

columns.headline: Senator Keel asks the Senate Clerk who may claim the room's record of March 27
columns.body: Senator Rufus Keel has asked Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, how the committee room's record of March 27, including the word taken down at 5:12 p.m., may be claimed. Mr. Pratt replied that it 'may be claimed by the speaker of the word, on identification.'

columns.headline: Seven couples remain at the 270th hour; the Arena's band reduced to six
columns.body: Seven couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 270th hour, two couples from Long Island City having retired before midnight. The management states that the ten-piece band 'has been reduced to six, by exhaustion.' Dr. Saul Weisz attends.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Matthias Strand recorded the first 22 bars of the carol at Union Seminary at 4 p.m.; the record sails Saturday on the Aquitania.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 58. Thursday. Ball game at last. Mrs. Ruth sat on the third-base side.

lead.headline: The Babe answers the bell first time up, and the Stadium rings off the hook
lead.deck: Married Wednesday, homers Thursday; Number 3 sends one into the stands in the first and doffs his cap to Mrs. Ruth; Yankees seven, Boston three
lead.body: At half past three this afternoon the Yankees finally took the field in their numbers, and in the first inning Number 3 hit Boston's pitching into the stands, rounded the bases, and doffed his cap to his bride of thirty-four hours in a box by third base. The Stadium's register, set up to measure the crowd against last year's, measured something it is still thinking about. Yankees seven, Boston three. Mr. Gehrig, Number 4, said nothing, as usual.

columns.headline: Senator Keel rings the vault, and the word won't come to the phone
columns.body: Senator Keel has asked the Senate Clerk who may claim the room's record of March twenty-seventh. Mr. Pratt says whoever said the word may have it, on identification. Nobody has come forward. The word 'resent' remains in the vault, where it is said to be keeping to itself.

columns.headline: Pike reels in two launches, and leaves North Beach on watch
columns.body: Mr. Pike has called in the launches off Hallett's Point and College Point, WORS having said nothing for a week. The North Beach launch stays. Its crew have asked for a bigger net. Only thirty-one people rang the Exchange about WORS last night. Queens is getting over it.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: St. Gregory's switches off, and society tunes in anyway
columns.body: Darlings, the Babe's wedding was the one event this spring that nobody recorded, which has made it the most talked about. Sixty of us stood on the steps at half past five. We could hear the organ. We could not hear the vows. We made them up.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Strand's twenty-two bars sail Saturday on the Aquitania, in a cabin next to nobody.

lead.headline: Yankees beat Boston 7 to 3 at the opening; crowd's sound measured at 31 points
lead.deck: About 45,000 at the Stadium; Mr. Ruth's home run in the first measured against 27 points for last year's loudest; the register 'at its stop' for nine seconds
lead.body: The Yankees beat the Boston club 7 to 3 at the Stadium yesterday before about 45,000, the players wearing numbers for the first time in a championship game. Mr. Ruth hit a home run in the first inning. The Stadium's sound register, read by the club's engineer, Mr. Walter Dunphy, measured the crowd at that moment at 31 points, against 27 points for the loudest moment of last year's home opening, and held 'at its stop' for nine seconds.

columns.headline: Sergeant Moran's watch at the Corona grocer's discontinued; warrant stands
columns.body: Detective Sergeant Edward Moran states that his watch at Mr. Isidore Lippman's grocery on 104th Street, Corona, kept on two Thursdays from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m., is discontinued, no purchaser of the Portland sardine having called. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Six couples remain at the 294th hour; Mrs. Corrigan 'asks for nothing'
columns.body: Six couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 294th hour, the management states. Dr. Saul Weisz states that Mrs. Margaret Corrigan 'asks for nothing and accepts soup.' Mr. Leo Gant has been cautioned twice for humming during the rest period.

columns.headline: Licence hearings open Monday at Borough Hall; 412 forms returned
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane, Deputy Secretary of State, will hear the first applications for licences under the Listening Act at the Queens Borough Hall at 10 a.m. Monday. Of 6,000 forms delivered on April 9, 412 have been returned, 97 of them with the date of installation left blank.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night; the Exchange logged 12 inquiries, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 63. Friday. The Babe's homer is still going. Somewhere over the Bronx.

lead.headline: Number 3 turns the Stadium up to thirty-one, and the needle begs for mercy
lead.deck: Mr. Dunphy's register gives the Babe's first-inning homer four points more than last year's best and sits at its stop for nine seconds; the true figure, he says, may be higher
lead.body: The Stadium's sound register, which Mr. Dunphy reads the way a doctor reads a chest, gave yesterday's crowd thirty-one points when the Babe's first-inning homer went in, against last year's best of twenty-seven, and stayed at its stop for nine seconds, which is as loud as the machine goes. Mr. Dunphy says the true figure may be higher, the needle being unable to say. The Babe says he did not hear a thing. He was looking at a box by third base.

columns.headline: Party Line holds for the four o'clock, and nobody's calling
columns.body: Three Fridays now. Party Line was in the parcel window at four, washed and waiting, and nothing came. Sergeant Moran has given up his Thursdays at the Corona grocer's. The lineman's warrant stands. She stayed till six, then went to the warm end of the board.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'How old is my wiring, and who's asking?'
columns.body: Sir, ninety-seven of the first four hundred and twelve licence forms came back with the date of installation left blank, because nobody knows it. The hearings open Monday. The operator suggests you write 'before me,' which is true of every building in Queens and most landlords.

columns.headline: Six couples left, and Mr. Gant is cautioned for broadcasting in the rest hour
columns.body: Six couples at two this morning. Mr. Gant has been warned twice for humming during the rest, the rules requiring rest to be quiet. He says it is the only way Mrs. Corrigan can sleep. Mrs. Corrigan asks for nothing and accepts soup. The soup has asked for a raise.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Twelve calls about WORS to the Exchange last night. A week ago it was ninety. Queens has a short memory and a long night.

record.ear: Fair, windy. High 61. Low 44. Smoke over Corona.

lead.headline: Fire in the Corona ash dumps spreads over 40 acres; smoke over Elmhurst
lead.deck: Discovered at 2:20 p.m. near the Flushing River; five engine companies pump from the creek; the Brooklyn Ash Removal Co. 'cannot say' how it began
lead.body: Fire broke out in the Corona ash dumps near the Flushing River at 2:20 p.m. yesterday and by 9 p.m. had spread over about 40 acres of the heaps, the Fire Department states. Five engine companies pumped water from Flushing Creek through the night. A west wind carried smoke over Elmhurst and Jackson Heights, from which 140 subscribers telephoned the Exchange. A reopened walk-up on the ash road reported smoke at its windows. The Brooklyn Ash Removal Co. 'cannot say' how the fire began.

columns.headline: Week's count: 940 night calls on the tone; Dr. Rastin's meter 'as before'
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 940 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, against 1,130 the week before. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles as before.

columns.headline: Five couples remain at the 318th hour of the Jamaica marathon
columns.body: Five couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 318th hour, a Richmond Hill couple having retired at 4:40 p.m. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan and Mr. Leo Gant continue, with couples from Ridgewood, Astoria and Sunnyside and a couple 'from New Jersey.'

columns.headline: No decision on the Riverhead seal this week, the Appellate clerk states
columns.body: The clerk of the Appellate Division states that no decision on Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Board of Elections' Riverhead record will be handed down this week. Mr. Gorman has attended the court on each of the four days it sat.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The ash dump fire was reported 'held but not out' at 3 a.m., Deputy Chief Martin Shea states.

speaker.ear: Windy. High 61. Saturday. Corona's on fire again. Corona says it's the spring.

lead.headline: Corona's ash heaps light up, and the borough gets smoke on the line
lead.deck: Forty acres of dump go up by the Flushing River; five engines pump the creek all night; Jackson Heights rings the Exchange a hundred and forty times to say it can smell it
lead.body: Every spring the Corona ash dumps catch fire, and every spring the Brooklyn Ash Removal Company cannot say how. This year it was twenty past two yesterday afternoon, forty acres by nine, and five engine companies pumping Flushing Creek at the heaps until the creek ran low. The west wind took the smoke to Jackson Heights, which rang the Exchange a hundred and forty times to say so. Deputy Chief Shea says the fire is held but not out. The ash men say it will smoulder till June.

columns.headline: The Hum loses its callers, but keeps its pitch
columns.body: Nine hundred and forty calls this week about the night tone, down from eleven hundred. Dr. Rastin's meter on 31st Street still reads forty-one, at the same strength. The light company has stopped claiming credit and started saying nothing, which it does very well.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Nine nights off the air, and the borough's ears wander
columns.body: WORS has been quiet nine nights. Last night the Exchange took four calls about it, one from a man who wanted to know whether it was WORS that had stopped or his set. It was WORS. He seemed relieved, then disappointed. Pin ninety-seven is gathering dust.

columns.headline: Five couples left, and New Jersey is still on the line
columns.body: Richmond Hill sat down at twenty to five, leaving five: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant, Ridgewood, Astoria, Sunnyside, and a pair from New Jersey who will not say which part. The crowd boos them gently every hour. They have begun to bow.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Strand's twenty-two bars sailed at five past eleven on the Aquitania. Wales has been told to sit down.

lead.headline: Mrs. Hattie Brennan, operator at the Astoria exchange for 38 years, dies at 61
lead.deck: Took her first call in 1891; trained 'about 400' operators; the Astoria board to make no connections for one minute at 10 a.m. Tuesday
lead.body: Mrs. Hattie Brennan, who took calls at the Astoria exchange for 38 years, died on Friday at her home on 30th Avenue, Astoria, of pneumonia, aged 61. She took her first call in 1891 and trained, by the exchange's count, about 400 operators. Superintendent Wilfred Arne states that the Astoria board will make no connections for one minute at 10 a.m. Tuesday, the hour of the funeral mass at St. Joseph's. Mrs. Brennan is survived by two daughters, both operators.

columns.headline: Ice to rise to 45 cents the hundredweight on May 1, Astoria Lake Ice Co. states
columns.body: The Astoria Lake Ice Co. will raise the price of ice delivered by wagon from 40 to 45 cents the hundredweight on May 1, its manager, Mr. Gustave Pohl, states, citing 'the cost of feed.' The company's horse Major, 22 years on the Steinway route, retired yesterday.

columns.headline: Ash dump fire held on 26 of its 40 acres; smoke continues over Corona
columns.body: Deputy Chief Martin Shea of the Fire Department states that the fire in the Corona ash dumps was burning on about 26 of its 40 acres at 6 p.m. yesterday and was held there, two engine companies remaining. Smoke continued over Corona and Elmhurst. The Exchange logged 61 calls.

columns.headline: Four couples remain at the 342nd hour; the New Jersey couple retires
columns.body: Four couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 342nd hour, the couple 'from New Jersey' having retired at 10:05 p.m. without stating its town. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan and Mr. Leo Gant and couples from Ridgewood, Astoria and Sunnyside continue.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reported 'all well, 58 below' at 10:24 p.m.; the camp acknowledged the opening day score.

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 57. Sunday. Ice goes up a nickel. Your drip tray goes up nothing.

lead.headline: Major hangs up his harness, and the Steinway ice route loses its best operator
lead.deck: Twenty-two years on the wagon, every stop by heart; the ice company retires him the week it puts ice up a nickel; Steinway Street's kitchens send down carrots
lead.body: Major, a grey of about twenty-six who has pulled the Astoria Lake Ice Company's wagon up Steinway Street since 1907, retired yesterday to a field in Bayside. He knew every stop. He connected every kitchen on the route to its ice without being told, and stopped at houses that had cancelled years ago, out of loyalty. On his last morning the kitchens sent down carrots. The company puts ice up a nickel on the first of May, citing the cost of feed. Major will be eating free.

columns.headline: Last call for Mrs. Brennan, and the Astoria board will go quiet for her
columns.body: Mrs. Hattie Brennan took her first call at the Astoria exchange in 1891 and trained about four hundred operators, ours among them. She died on Friday, aged sixty-one. On Tuesday at ten the Astoria board will connect nobody for one minute. Please do not ring then.

columns.headline: The ash heaps simmer down to twenty-six acres, and Corona is still fuming
columns.body: The Corona dump fire was held at twenty-six acres last night, with two engines left pumping the creek. Sixty-one more calls about the smoke. The ash company still cannot say how it started. The ash, being ash, is not saying either.

columns.headline: New Jersey signs off at five past ten, and four couples stay tuned
columns.body: The pair from New Jersey sat down at five past ten and left without saying which town, to the end. Four couples remain: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant, Ridgewood, Astoria and Sunnyside. The crowd stood and booed them out with real affection. They bowed.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America is fifty-eight below and has heard the opening day score. It sends congratulations to Number 3, and to Mrs. Number 3.

lead.headline: First licence hearings under the Listening Act open at Borough Hall at 10 a.m.
lead.deck: Deputy Secretary of State Crane to hear 40 applicants a day; 108 owners report systems installed before any record of installation; the hearing room's own system unlicensed
lead.body: Mr. Hollis Crane, Deputy Secretary of State, opens the first hearings on applications for licences under the Listening Act at 10 a.m. today in Room 2 of the Queens Borough Hall, and will hear 40 applicants a day. Of 588 forms returned by Saturday, 108 give the date of installation as unknown or 'before the present owner.' Mr. Crane stated that the hearing room's own house system, installed in 1916, 'is not yet licensed and will be heard first.'

columns.headline: Yankees beat Boston 4 to 2 Saturday and lose 5 to 3 Sunday at the Stadium
columns.body: The Yankees beat the Boston club 4 to 2 at the Stadium on Saturday, Mr. Lou Gehrig hitting a home run, and lost 5 to 3 yesterday before about 30,000. The Brooklyn club lost twice at Philadelphia. The Stadium's register measured Saturday's crowd at 22 points 'at most.'

columns.headline: Three couples remain at the 366th hour; a Sunnyside couple retires
columns.body: Three couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 366th hour, the Sunnyside couple having retired at 3:30 p.m. Sunday. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan and Mr. Leo Gant, Mr. and Mrs. Stanley Novak of Ridgewood and a couple from Astoria continue.

columns.headline: Corona ash dump fire declared out at 4 p.m. Sunday; the heaps to smoulder
columns.body: Deputy Chief Martin Shea states that the fire in the Corona ash dumps was declared out at 4 p.m. yesterday, the last engine company withdrawing, but that the heaps 'will smoulder for some weeks, as in other years.' The Brooklyn Ash Removal Co. has placed four watchmen.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power will announce 'a revision of rates' at noon today, the company's secretary states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 64. Monday. Your building has to answer some questions today. So does your landlord.

lead.headline: Landlords form a party line at Borough Hall, and the hearing room goes first
lead.deck: Mr. Crane starts on forty applicants a day; a hundred and eight can't say when their buildings were wired; the room he sits in isn't licensed either
lead.body: At ten this morning Mr. Crane of the Secretary of State's office sat down in Room 2 at Borough Hall to license the borough's ears, and the landlords were already up the stairs and round the corner. A hundred and eight of them have written on their forms that they do not know when their buildings started listening. One wrote 'before my father.' Mr. Crane began by licensing his own room, which was wired in 1916 and has been hearing hearings unlicensed ever since. It passed.

columns.headline: Gehrig goes deep, and the Stadium's register stays on low volume
columns.body: Saturday the Yankees beat Boston four to two, Mr. Gehrig homering, and the register gave the crowd twenty-two points at most, which is about a church picnic. Yesterday Boston won five to three. Brooklyn lost two at Philadelphia, and nobody measured that. Nobody wanted to.

columns.headline: Three couples left, and the Novaks of Ridgewood dance in perfect harmony
columns.body: Sunnyside sat down on Sunday afternoon, leaving three: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant, a couple from Astoria, and Mr. and Mrs. Novak of Ridgewood, married eleven years and not speaking since the hundredth hour. Mrs. Novak says it helps. Mr. Novak was not asked.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Eleven nights off the air, and nobody rang
columns.body: WORS has now been silent eleven nights. Last night the Exchange took no calls about it at all. Not one. The operator waited until two in case. The North Beach launch is still out. Its crew report flounder, and a feeling they cannot describe.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Crane licensed nine buildings today and adjourned one, which answered 'unknown' to every question, including the owner's name.

lead.headline: Queens Light & Power to raise its domestic rate to 7.5 cents from May 1
lead.deck: Half a cent the kilowatt-hour; the company cites 'the expense of the Astoria inspection and adjustments'; Alderman Feeney to ask the Commission to suspend the increase
lead.body: Queens Light & Power will raise its domestic rate from 7 cents to 7.5 cents the kilowatt-hour on all bills from May 1, Mr. Roland Tisch announced for the company at noon yesterday. The company cites 'the expense of the Astoria inspection and of routine adjustments since.' Asked what had been adjusted, Mr. Tisch replied that the adjustments were 'routine.' Alderman John Feeney stated that he will ask the Public Service Commission to suspend the increase. The Commission sits next on May 14.

columns.headline: Licence hearings: nine granted, one adjourned for want of an owner's name
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted nine licences under the Listening Act at the Borough Hall yesterday, the first in the State. One application, for a house system on Northern Boulevard, was adjourned, the form answering 'unknown' to every question, including the name of the owner. Forty applicants are listed today.

columns.headline: Astoria exchange to make no connections from 10 a.m. to 10:01 a.m. today
columns.body: Superintendent Wilfred Arne states that the Astoria board will make no connections from 10 a.m. to 10:01 a.m. today during the funeral mass of Mrs. Hattie Brennan at St. Joseph's, Astoria. Subscribers are asked not to signal. Calls in progress 'will be held, not cut.'

columns.headline: Two couples remain at the 390th hour; the Astoria couple retires at 7:50 p.m.
columns.body: Two couples remained on the Jamaica Arena floor at 2 a.m. today, the marathon's 390th hour, the Astoria couple having retired at 7:50 p.m. yesterday. Mrs. Margaret Corrigan and Mr. Leo Gant and Mr. and Mrs. Stanley Novak of Ridgewood continue.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power states that the revision of rates 'does not concern any tone.'

speaker.ear: Showers. High 59. Tuesday. The light company wants another half cent. For what, it won't say.

lead.headline: Light company turns up the volume on the bill, and won't say what's playing
lead.deck: Half a cent more the kilowatt-hour from May Day, to pay for adjusting nothing at Astoria; Feeney goes to the Commission; Dolan says he could have told them
lead.body: From the first of May Queens Light & Power will charge seven and a half cents the kilowatt-hour instead of seven, and Mr. Tisch says the extra half is for the Astoria inspection and the routine adjustments since. The company has never said what it adjusted, there being, by its own account, nothing to adjust. So Queens will now pay half a cent more for nothing. Alderman Feeney is going to the Commission to stop it. Mr. Dolan says he warned everyone in 1926. Nobody can find the warning.

columns.headline: The Astoria board puts Queens on hold for Mrs. Brennan
columns.body: At ten this morning the Astoria exchange connected nobody for one minute while Mrs. Brennan's mass was said at St. Joseph's. Calls in progress were held, not cut, as she would have done it. The operators she trained bowed their heads at their boards. Nobody signalled. Queens can be decent.

columns.headline: Two couples left, and the Arena gets ready to play the last dance back
columns.body: Astoria sat down at ten to eight last night. Two couples remain: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant, and the Novaks of Ridgewood, who still are not speaking. The management has had its machine overhauled, in case the finish is close. Nobody at the Arena now remembers the first week.

columns.headline: Licence hearings: nine buildings pass, and one won't say who's calling
columns.body: Mr. Crane licensed nine buildings yesterday, the first in the State, and adjourned a tenth on Northern Boulevard whose form said 'unknown' to every question, owner included. Somebody posted it. The envelope had no stamp. Mr. Crane has asked the Post Office who carried it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Alderman Feeney's letter to the Commission went by hand at four. Duke carried it as far as the corner.

record.ear: Fair. High 62. Low 47. Passover begins at sundown.

lead.headline: Jamaica marathon ends at 1:12 a.m., 413th hour; both couples down 'together'
lead.deck: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Novak fall at the same moment, the judges state; the prize of 1,000 dollars reserved until the Arena's record is played back Saturday
lead.body: The dance marathon at the Jamaica Arena ended at 1:12 a.m. today in its 413th hour, when Mrs. Margaret Corrigan, dancing with Mr. Leo Gant, and Mr. Stanley Novak, dancing with Mrs. Novak, went down 'together, in the judges' opinion,' the management states. About 2,600 persons were present. The prize of 1,000 dollars is reserved until the Arena's record of the final minute has been played back before both couples at 3 p.m. Saturday. Dr. Saul Weisz attended both.

columns.headline: Licence hearings: 31 granted; 11 owners name Vantry & Co. 'by belief'
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 31 licences under the Listening Act at the Borough Hall yesterday. The owners of 14 buildings stated that they 'cannot say who installed' their systems, 11 of them naming Vantry & Co. 'by belief.' Mr. Crane accepted 'Vantry & Co., by belief' as an answer.

columns.headline: Passover begins at sundown; the Exchange expects 2,000 long-distance calls
columns.body: Passover begins at sundown tonight. Kosher butchers report the heaviest trade since 1925, and the Exchange expects about 2,000 long-distance calls from Queens between 6 p.m. and 8 p.m., chiefly to Chicago, Cleveland and Columbus. Matzoth sell at 25 cents the pound.

columns.headline: North Beach launch withdrawn; the Radio Division to 'listen from shore'
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that the launch off North Beach was withdrawn yesterday, WORS 1610 not having been heard since 11:16 p.m. on April 10, and that the Division 'will listen from shore.' The Exchange has logged no inquiries since Saturday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Margaret Corrigan was carried from the Arena floor at 1:20 a.m. and states that she 'will dance Saturday if asked.'

speaker.ear: Fair. High 62. Wednesday. Passover tonight. A good holiday to all who keep it.

lead.headline: Marathon ends in a dead heat, and a thousand dollars waits on the playback
lead.deck: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Novak go down at twelve past one, together, say the judges; the record of the last minute to be played Saturday before both couples and a peanut man
lead.body: At twelve minutes past one this morning, in the four hundred and thirteenth hour, Mrs. Corrigan's knees went and Mr. Novak's knees went, and the judges, three tired men in straw hats, said they went together. None of the crowd could say otherwise. The management has reserved the thousand dollars until Saturday, when the Arena will play back the final minute before both couples. Mr. Gant says the record will hear Mrs. Corrigan last. Mrs. Novak, speaking at last, says it will not.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike pulls in the last launch and keeps an ear to the shore
columns.body: The North Beach launch came in at six last night, its crew sunburnt and carrying flounder. WORS has been silent since the tenth. Nobody has rung the Exchange about it since Saturday. Mr. Pike will listen from shore. So, it seems, will nobody else.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the long lines pass over my call tonight?'
columns.body: Madam, the Exchange expects two thousand long-distance calls between six and eight tonight, to Chicago, Cleveland and Columbus mostly. Book now, not at five to eight. The operator will put you through and will not listen to the blessing, though she may say amen.

columns.headline: Landlords can't trace the line, so the State takes Vantry on trust
columns.body: Thirty-one licences went out yesterday. Fourteen landlords could not say who wired their buildings, and eleven of them wrote 'Vantry and Company, by belief.' Mr. Crane accepted it. Vantry and Company has not been asked, there being nobody there to ask.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Corrigan was carried out at twenty past one and says she will dance on Saturday if asked. Mr. Gant says she will not be asked.

lead.headline: Summons in the luncheonette's suit still unserved; hearing set for Monday
lead.deck: Process server reports three visits to the company's listed box; the news stand's renewal of March 23 'not found' in the County Clerk's register; notices to vacate fall due May 1
lead.body: The summons in Mr. Oscar Bliss's suit against Signal Ground Rents Inc. remains unserved four days before Monday's hearing in the Municipal Court at Long Island City, the process server, Mr. Felix Raab, having called three times at the company's post office box and found it 'not rented.' The proprietor of the Arcade's news and cigar stand states that his renewal of March 23 is not in the County Clerk's register of leases. Notices to vacate served on ten tenants fall due on May 1.

columns.headline: Seder in Kew Gardens recorded for a son in Ohio; 14 sides by parcel post
columns.body: Mr. and Mrs. Abraham Feld of Kew Gardens recorded their seder last night on 14 sides for their son, Mr. Samuel Feld, in Cleveland, Ohio. The records go by parcel post today. Mr. Feld stated that the youngest grandchild 'asked the four questions twice, the first time too fast.'

columns.headline: Feeney and Dolan to debate at Long Island City High School tonight
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney and former Commissioner Augustin Dolan, rival candidates for borough president, will debate at the Long Island City High School at 8 p.m. tonight. The school's system will record the debate, and the record will be played in this newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue from noon tomorrow.

columns.headline: Licence hearings: 38 granted Wednesday; a queue in the corridor by 7 a.m.
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 38 licences under the Listening Act yesterday. Owners began queueing in the Borough Hall corridor at 7 a.m., about 90 being present when the room opened at 10 a.m. Those without forms are 'sent to the end and given one.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Long-distance calls from Queens between 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. last night numbered 2,214, the Exchange states, 812 of them to Ohio.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 70. Thursday. Spring has picked up the receiver at last.

lead.headline: Kew Gardens puts the seder on the record, and Cleveland gets it by post
lead.deck: Mr. Samuel Feld can't come home for Passover, so home goes to him: fourteen sides of the Feld seder, the youngest asking twice
lead.body: Mr. Samuel Feld draws bridges for a living in Cleveland, Ohio, and could not get home this year, so last night his parents in Kew Gardens put the whole seder on the record for him: the blessings, the four questions, his Uncle Morris's opinion of the horseradish, and his mother asking whether he is eating. Fourteen sides. The youngest grandchild asked the four questions twice, the first time too fast. The records went by parcel post this morning. Mrs. Feld put in a letter. It says he should telephone.

columns.headline: Bliss's summons can't get through, and the news stand's lease has no listing
columns.body: Mr. Raab, process server, has called three times at Signal Ground Rents' post box. It is not rented. The news stand's renewal is not in the County Clerk's book either. The hearing is Monday. The notices fall due Wednesday. Nobody at the company will be told, because nobody is.

columns.headline: Feeney and Dolan square off tonight, and both will be on the record
columns.body: Alderman Feeney and Mr. Dolan debate at eight tonight at Long Island City High School, and the school will record every word. The Record will play it in its Jackson Avenue window from noon tomorrow. The Speaker will tell you which bits to listen to. Duke is expected.

columns.headline: Licence queue forms at seven, and Borough Hall gets the busy signal
columns.body: Ninety landlords were in the Borough Hall corridor by the time Mr. Crane opened his door at ten, some since seven, all with forms. Those without forms are sent to the end of the line and given one, then wait again. Thirty-eight licences granted. The corridor hums.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Eight hundred and twelve calls to Ohio last night. Ohio has never been so blessed, or so expensive.

lead.headline: Candidates debate 94 minutes; Mr. Dolan proposes an office 'to hear the ground'
lead.deck: About 1,100 at Long Island City High School; the Alderman on the light rate, the former Commissioner on the sewers; the school's record to be played in this newspaper's window from noon
lead.body: Alderman John Feeney and former Commissioner Augustin Dolan debated for 94 minutes before about 1,100 persons at the Long Island City High School last night. The record of the hall has Mr. Feeney at 8:21 p.m.: 'I will not have Queens pay half a cent for a noise.' Mr. Dolan, at 8:47 p.m.: 'I propose a borough office to hear the ground, and to say what it hears.' At 9:30 p.m. the hall's record contains a dog.

columns.headline: Letter from the National Library of Wales delivered to Dr. Strand
columns.body: A letter from the National Library of Wales, posted April 16, was delivered to Dr. Matthias Strand yesterday. Dr. Strand stated that it 'asks two questions and answers none,' and that he will reply when the Library has heard the 22 bars, due at Southampton today.

columns.headline: Mr. Crane grants 44 licences; the Northern Boulevard application struck out
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 44 licences yesterday, 122 in four days. The application for a house system on Northern Boulevard adjourned on Monday, its form answering 'unknown' to every question, was struck out, no owner appearing. Mr. Crane stated that the system 'remains unlicensed and in operation.'

columns.headline: St. Mary's to admit Dr. Rastin's meter to the church on a weeknight in May
columns.body: The rectory of St. Mary's, Long Island City, states that Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia will be admitted to the church on a weeknight in May 'with his meter and in silence,' to measure the tone recorded on the Holy Saturday record at 41 cycles. No date is fixed.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Alderman Feeney's terrier was removed from the debate stage at 9:31 p.m. and returned at 9:34 p.m., the school's record states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 66. Friday. Two men argued for ninety-four minutes. A dog won.

lead.headline: Feeney and Dolan cross wires, and Duke gets the last word
lead.deck: A half cent for a noise, says the Alderman; an office to hear the ground, says the Commissioner; at half past nine the terrier takes the stage and the hall's record takes him down
lead.body: Last night at Long Island City High School Alderman Feeney and Mr. Dolan argued for ninety-four minutes before eleven hundred people. The Alderman said Queens would not pay half a cent for a noise. Mr. Dolan said he would open a borough office to hear the ground and say what it heard, which got the biggest cheer of the night. At half past nine Duke walked onto the stage, barked once at Mr. Dolan, and was removed. He was back in three minutes.

columns.headline: Party Line waits by the window, and Corona still doesn't call
columns.body: Four Fridays now. Party Line sat in the parcel window at four with her paws together, and at six she got down. The Jamaica tin is still in Sergeant Moran's drawer. The lineman's warrant still stands. The warm end of the board is warmer now it's spring.

columns.headline: Wales writes two questions, no answers, and Strand rings off till the bars land
columns.body: The National Library's letter reached Dr. Strand yesterday. He says it asks two questions and answers none. He will not say what the questions are. His twenty-two bars land at Southampton today. Until then he is humming the twenty-third to himself to keep it warm.

columns.headline: Northern Boulevard's nobody gets struck out, and stays on the air
columns.body: Mr. Crane struck out the application from the Northern Boulevard building whose form said 'unknown' to everything, no owner appearing. The system is now unlicensed, which it always was, and in operation, which it always is. Mr. Crane has written it a letter. It has not written back.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Record's window played the debate to about four hundred people this afternoon. Duke's bark got a round of applause.

lead.headline: Week's count: 166 licences granted under the Act; 1,212 forms returned
lead.deck: Mr. Crane sat five days; 241 owners give the installation date as unknown; the corridor queue reached 140 on Friday; hearings resume Monday with 60 a day
lead.body: Mr. Hollis Crane, Deputy Secretary of State, granted 166 licences under the Listening Act at the Queens Borough Hall in the five days to Friday, adjourned 19 and struck out two, his office states. Of 1,212 forms returned, 241 give the date of installation as unknown. The queue in the Borough Hall corridor reached 140 at 9 a.m. yesterday. Mr. Crane will hear 60 applicants a day from Monday. About 4,800 forms delivered on April 9 have not been returned. Licences are required from July 1.

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,186 night calls on the tone, the first rise since March
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,186 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 940 the week before, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. Dr. Emil Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles 'as before.'

columns.headline: Debate record played to about 2,300 at the Jackson Avenue window
columns.body: The record of the Feeney-Dolan debate was played in this newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue three times yesterday, at noon, 3 p.m. and 6 p.m., to about 2,300 persons in all. The record will be played once more at noon today.

columns.headline: Aquitania docks at Southampton; Dr. Strand's record sent on to Aberystwyth
columns.body: The Cunard Line states that the Aquitania docked at Southampton at 4 p.m. yesterday and that Dr. Matthias Strand's record of the first 22 bars of the WORS 1610 carol has been sent on to the National Library of Wales at Aberystwyth by rail.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power states that the rise in night calls 'is not related to the revision of rates.'

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 60. Saturday. The Hum is back on the switchboard. It never left the wire.

lead.headline: The Arena plays back the last minute, and both knees hit the same note
lead.deck: Two thousand pay a quarter to hear four hundred and thirteen hours end; the record hears Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Novak go down in one sound; the judges split the thousand
lead.body: At three this afternoon the Jamaica Arena played back the last minute of its marathon to both couples, three judges, Dr. Weisz and two thousand people who paid a quarter each. Then came one thump, a single sound, and the room went quiet, because a record cannot lie about knees. The judges conferred for eleven minutes and split the prize, five hundred dollars to each couple. Mrs. Corrigan wept. Mrs. Novak spoke to Mr. Novak for the first time in three hundred hours. He has not repeated it.

columns.headline: The Hum's callers ring back in, and the light company hangs up on the question
columns.body: Eleven hundred and eighty-six calls about the night tone this week, up from nine hundred and forty, the first rise since March. The company says it has nothing to do with the new rate. Nobody had suggested it did, until the company said so.

columns.headline: A hundred and sixty-six licences out, and forty-eight hundred forms gone quiet
columns.body: Mr. Crane granted a hundred and sixty-six licences this week and sat through two hundred and forty-one landlords who cannot say when their buildings were wired. Four thousand eight hundred forms are still out. The corridor queue reached a hundred and forty. Mr. Crane has started bringing lunch.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Sixteen nights of dead air, and the map gets dusted
columns.body: WORS has said nothing since the tenth. The launches are home. Nobody rings. This morning the office boy took down our map of Queens to wash the wall, and nobody asked where it had gone either. Pin ninety-seven is in a saucer on the editor's desk.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Strand's twenty-two bars are on the train to Aberystwyth. The guard has been asked not to hum.

lead.headline: Marathon prize divided after the record of the final minute is played back
lead.deck: Played at 3:04 p.m. before both couples and about 2,000; the judges find 'one sound'; 500 dollars each to Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant and to Mr. and Mrs. Novak
lead.body: The management of the Jamaica Arena played its record of the final minute of the dance marathon at 3:04 p.m. yesterday before both finishing couples, the judges and about 2,000 spectators. The judges stated that the record contained 'one sound, not two,' at the moment both couples went down at 1:12 a.m. on April 24. The prize of 1,000 dollars was divided, 500 dollars to Mrs. Margaret Corrigan and Mr. Leo Gant and 500 dollars to Mr. and Mrs. Stanley Novak of Ridgewood.

columns.headline: Woodhaven hardware dog answers the shop's telephone, the Exchange states
columns.body: The Queens Exchange states that calls to Mr. Herman Lutz's hardware store in Woodhaven are being answered when the shop is shut by Mr. Lutz's collie, Pal, who lifts the receiver from its hook and barks twice. Operators will connect callers 'and say what they are connected to.'

columns.headline: Little America asks the result of 'the dance at Jamaica'; replies 'fair'
columns.body: The Navy's station at Bay Shore heard Little America at 10:16 p.m. yesterday, the camp reporting 'all well, 61 below' and asking the result of 'the dance at Jamaica.' The station sent the result. The camp replied 'fair.'

columns.headline: Mrs. Grieve's members to seal their capsule June 15; No. 23 'where it was'
columns.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve states that the thirteen members who left the Phonautograph Society will seal their capsule at the Flushing Free Library on June 15, and have again asked Mr. Cyril Abbot for record No. 23. Mr. Abbot replied that the record 'is where it was.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Margaret Corrigan states that she will spend her share on shoes.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 63. Sunday. A collie in Woodhaven answers the telephone. Better than some.

lead.headline: Woodhaven's best operator has four legs, and picks up on the second ring
lead.deck: Pal the collie lifts the hardware store's receiver when the shop is shut and barks twice; the Exchange tells callers what they've reached; one order taken, by our count
lead.body: Mr. Herman Lutz shuts his hardware store on Jamaica Avenue at six, and from six on, when the telephone rings, his collie Pal gets up, knocks the receiver off its hook with his nose, and barks twice into it. The Exchange now warns callers what they are connected to. A lady in Richmond Hill told Pal that she wanted a dozen brass hooks, and rang Mr. Lutz next morning to ask whether the dog had passed it on. Mr. Lutz said he had. Pal has asked for a commission.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who's barking on my line?'
columns.body: Sir, if you ring Lutz's hardware after six you are connected to Pal, a collie, and the operator will say so first. Speak slowly. He barks twice, which means the shop is shut. He has never yet barked once, and we would rather not know what that means.

columns.headline: Byrd's men tune in to the Jamaica result, and score it fair at sixty-one below
columns.body: Little America came through last night at sixty-one below and asked how the dance at Jamaica came out. Bay Shore told them: a dead heat, the prize split. The camp replied 'fair,' which from men who have been dancing round a stove all winter is high praise.

columns.headline: Mrs. Grieve sets her capsule for June, and No. 23 hasn't moved a groove
columns.body: The thirteen who walked out of the Phonautograph Society will seal their capsule at Flushing on June fifteenth. Mrs. Grieve has written to Mr. Abbot for record No. 23 a second time. He replied that it is where it was. She has asked where that is. He has not replied.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Corrigan will spend her two hundred and fifty on shoes. Mr. Gant will spend his on silence.

lead.headline: Commission to hear the Feeney petition against the light rate on May 14
lead.deck: To sit with its reserved finding on the two Astoria readings of 41 cycles; the increase of half a cent to take effect Wednesday 'pending the hearing'; Mr. Tisch: 'the rate concerns no tone'
lead.body: The Public Service Commission will hear Alderman John Feeney's petition to suspend Queens Light & Power's increase in its domestic rate at its sitting of May 14, Commissioner Maurice Lacey's office states, the same sitting at which the Commission will give its reserved finding on the two Astoria readings of 41 cycles. The increase, from 7 cents to 7.5 cents the kilowatt-hour, takes effect on Wednesday 'pending the hearing.' Mr. Roland Tisch stated for the company that 'the rate concerns no tone.'

columns.headline: Yankees beat Washington 5 to 2; Sunday's game postponed; Brooklyn wins
columns.body: The Yankees beat the Washington club 5 to 2 at Griffith Stadium on Saturday, Mr. Tony Lazzeri hitting a home run, and Sunday's game at Washington was postponed for rain. The Brooklyn club beat the Boston Braves 6 to 3 at Ebbets Field yesterday before about 20,000.

columns.headline: Luncheonette suit to be heard at 10 a.m.; Signal Ground Rents not served
columns.body: Mr. Oscar Bliss's suit against Signal Ground Rents Inc. is set for 10 a.m. today before Judge Peter Hanrahan in the Municipal Court at Long Island City. The summons has not been served, the company's post office box being 'not rented.' The news stand's proprietor will testify.

columns.headline: Senate Clerk states the room's record of March 27 'remains unclaimed'
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27, including the word 'resent,' 'remains in the vault, unclaimed,' no one having identified the voice. Senator Rufus Keel has asked that the record be kept 'until the next session.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Pal, a collie, answered 46 calls to the Lutz hardware store in Woodhaven between 6 p.m. Saturday and midnight Sunday, the Exchange states.

speaker.ear: Rain. High 55. Monday. The luncheonette went to court. The landlord didn't. Nobody was surprised.

lead.headline: Bliss sues a landlord who never picks up, and the judge can't get a line
lead.deck: Judge Hanrahan adjourns to May 27 for want of service; the notice to vacate stayed for the luncheonette alone; the news stand tells the court his lease walked out of a locked drawer
lead.body: At ten this morning Mr. Bliss of the luncheonette stood up in the Municipal Court and sued a company that has no address and no telephone anyone answers. Judge Hanrahan asked whether the defendant was present. The court's own system was played back to confirm it was not. The judge adjourned to the twenty-seventh of May and stayed Mr. Bliss's notice to vacate till then. The news stand told the court his signed renewal went missing from a locked drawer. The judge asked who had the key. He did.

columns.headline: Lazzeri's number comes up at Washington, and Sunday gets washed off the air
columns.body: Five to two over Washington on Saturday, Mr. Lazzeri, Number 6, homering, and Sunday rained out. Brooklyn beat the Braves six to three at Ebbets Field before twenty thousand. Flatbush has asked for it to be played back, slowly, several times.

columns.headline: Pal works the weekend shift, and takes forty-six calls without a crossed wire
columns.body: Pal, Mr. Lutz's collie, answered forty-six calls between Saturday evening and midnight Sunday, barking twice each time. Three callers left orders. One proposed marriage, we are told to a wrong number. Mr. Lutz has had a cushion put under the telephone.

columns.headline: The Commission puts the light rate and the forty-one cycles on one line
columns.body: On May the fourteenth the Commission will hear Alderman Feeney against the half cent and give its ruling on the Astoria readings, both at one sitting. Mr. Tisch says the rate concerns no tone. The new rate starts Wednesday anyway. The tone started some time ago.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The nine other shops in the Arcade have till Wednesday. Mr. Bliss has offered them coffee and the name of his judge.

lead.headline: Luncheonette suit adjourned to May 27; notice stayed for Mr. Bliss alone
lead.deck: Judge Hanrahan finds the defendant 'not served and not present'; the news stand proprietor testifies his renewal was taken from a locked drawer; nine notices fall due tomorrow
lead.body: Judge Peter Hanrahan adjourned Mr. Oscar Bliss's suit against Signal Ground Rents Inc. to May 27 yesterday, the defendant being 'not served and not present,' the court's own record of the room confirming the second point. The notice to vacate served on Mr. Bliss's luncheonette was stayed until that date. The proprietor of the Arcade's news and cigar stand testified that his signed renewal was taken from a locked drawer to which he holds the only key. Nine other notices fall due tomorrow.

columns.headline: Light rate of 7.5 cents takes effect tomorrow; first bills read from May 6
columns.body: Queens Light & Power's domestic rate of 7.5 cents the kilowatt-hour takes effect tomorrow, the company states, the first bills at the new rate to be read from May 6. Alderman John Feeney's petition to suspend the increase will be heard by the Public Service Commission on May 14.

columns.headline: National Library of Wales cables receipt of the carol's first 22 bars
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand states that the National Library of Wales cabled yesterday that his record of the carol's first 22 bars had been received. The cable reads in full: 'RECEIVED. PLAYED WITH THE OTHER. WRITING.' Dr. Strand stated that he will 'wait for the post.'

columns.headline: Ice at 45 cents the hundredweight from tomorrow; three companies to raise
columns.body: Three Queens ice companies, the Astoria Lake Ice Co., the Jamaica Pond Ice Co. and the Flushing Bay Ice Co., will charge 45 cents the hundredweight delivered by wagon from tomorrow, against 40 cents, the managers state. Wagons will begin daily rounds on Monday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 has not been heard since 11:16 p.m. on April 10, the Radio Division states, in reply to an inquiry from this newspaper.

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 58. Tuesday. Tomorrow ice goes up, light goes up, and nine shops may go out.

lead.headline: Nine Arcade shops get the disconnect for May Day, and nobody pulls the plug
lead.deck: Tomorrow the notices fall due; the landlord sends no one; the luncheonette is stayed to the twenty-seventh and the news stand keeps the only key to a drawer that keeps nothing
lead.body: Tomorrow is the first of May, the day Signal Ground Rents Inc. told ten shops in the Vantry Arcade to be gone, and tonight nine of them do not know what to do. Nobody from the company has come to collect a key or change a lock. One tenant has packed half his stock and unpacked a quarter. Mr. Bliss is stayed to the twenty-seventh. The news stand holds the only key to an empty drawer. We will be there at nine.

columns.headline: Wales gets the full score, and cables back without the answer
columns.body: Aberystwyth cabled Dr. Strand yesterday: received, played with the other, writing. That is three things, and none of them is what Dr. Strand wants. The letter will take a week and a half. He says he has waited longer for less. He is still humming.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? We rang the Division ourselves, and got dead air back
columns.body: Nobody else was going to, so this newspaper rang the Radio Division today to ask about WORS. Not heard since the tenth, Mr. Pike said, and asked whether we had heard it. We had not. He seemed surprised anyone still wanted to know. So were we.

columns.headline: The light bill and the ice man both raise their pitch for May
columns.body: From tomorrow electricity is seven and a half cents the kilowatt-hour and ice is forty-five cents the hundredweight. The light company cites Astoria. The ice men cite oats. Your icebox and your lamp will both cost more to keep, and neither will work any better. Welcome to spring.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Alderman Feeney says he will be at the Arcade at nine tomorrow. So will Duke. So, we suspect, will nobody from Signal Ground Rents.
